hci1.title: Introduction to Human-Computer Interaction
hci1.content: What is HCI?Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) refers to the study and design of the interaction between people (users) and computers. It focuses on creating user-friendly interfaces and experiences. It is a multidisciplinary field that involves:Engineering – creating efficient systems and interfaces.Psychology – understanding user behavior and cognition.Design – making systems attractive and usable.Ergonomics – fitting the system to the human body and needs.HCI is about designing systems that allow people to interact with technology easily, efficiently, and safely.Why is it important?HCI is about doing things better. USABILITY (resulting interface are easy to use, efficient for the task, ensure safety and to correct completion of the task).Principles of HCI“Know Thy User”Understand the TaskReduce Memory LoadStrive for ConsistencyRemind Users and Refresh Their MemoryPrevent Errors/Reversal of ActionNaturalnessDetailed Breakdown of Principles1. “Know Thy User”Factors to Consider:AgeGenderEducation LevelSocial StatusBackground in Technology2. “Understand the Task”Design should match the steps and logic of the task the user wants to perform.3. Reduce Memory LoadUsers should not be required to memorize (or recall out of their heads) a great deal of information to carry out tasks.4. Strive for ConsistencyUsers should not have to wonder whether different words, situations, or actions mean the same thing. Don’t confuse your user. In other words, use all elements across your application consistently.5. Remind Users and Refresh Their MemoryAny significant task will involve the use of memory, so another good strategy is to employ interfaces that give continuous reminders of important information and thereby refresh the user’s memory.6. Prevent Errors/Reversal of ActionUsers hate errors, and even more so hate the feeling that they themselves have done something wrong. Either eliminate error-prone conditions or check for them and notify users about that before they commit to the action.Error Prevention:Error prevention over error correction.Automatic detection of errors.Clear error notifications.Offer solutions for problems.7. NaturalnessThe final major HCI principle is to favor “natural” interaction and interfaces. It follows from the free choice of modalities and may result in a human-computer interaction that is close to human-human communication.ConclusionHuman-Computer Interaction (HCI) plays a vital role in making technology easier, more effective, and more enjoyable to use. The principles of HCI guide us in designing interfaces that are not only visually appealing but also user-centered and efficient. As future designers and developers, we must always prioritize the user experience in everything we create.

hci2.title: Guidelines Categories and Example Guidelines
hci2.content: Characteristics of HCI GuidelinesHCI guidelines are more specific than general principles and are characterized by being:Task-basedUser-group focusedPlatform-dependentTypes of Guidelines (Categories)Guidelines are categorized to address different design contexts:User Type: Examples include kids, the elderly, and people with disabilities.Platform/System: Examples include mobile, desktop, embedded systems, and public kiosks.Vendor/Brand: Examples include iOS, Android, Windows, and company branding.Interaction Style: Examples include GUI, voice input, gesture, touchscreen, and haptics.Task Context: Examples include driving, shopping, outdoor use, and eyes-free scenarios.Application Type: Examples include games, e-commerce, social media, and navigation.The 9 General HCI Design Guidelines1. Visual Display LayoutFocuses on how to arrange elements on the screen:Avoid clutter.Use alignment and whitespace.Highlight key content at the top or center.Use consistent formatting.Example: U.S. government website design recommends placing clickable buttons near the top and center for easy access.2. Information Structuring & NavigationFocuses on how users move through and access information:Organize content logically (either hierarchically or sequentially).Use navigation aids like breadcrumbs, tabs, menus, sidebars, site maps, and search features.Key Navigation Patterns:Two-Panel Selector: A list is displayed on the left while corresponding details are displayed on the right.One-Window Drilldown: Tapping to move forward or back through screens (typical in mobile applications).3. Taking User InputDefined as Efficient and accurate input methods :Use drop-downs, radio buttons, and checkboxes to minimize typing.Use auto-complete or suggested values.Minimize typing to proactively reduce user errors.Use default values.Avoid placing conflicting buttons too close together (e.g., placing Submit and Cancel side-by-side).Example: A calendar form utilizing structured input fields (such as separate day, month, and year dropdowns) reduces user error.4. Design for Users with DisabilitiesRooted in the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG 2.0) framework:Provide text alternatives for images.Allow keyboard-only navigation (essential for users who cannot use a mouse or touchscreen).Avoid flashing content to eliminate seizure risks.Use captions for video and audio.Make color and contrast adjustable.Example: Websites built with high-contrast themes and adjustable font sizes for visually impaired users.5. Design for Mobile DevicesAddresses specific physical and screen constraints (small screen, varying orientations, and touch input):Minimize typing.Use larger touch areas that are thumb-friendly.Optimize screen space using scrollable panels or tabs.Keep users focused with clear paths.Example: Android's multi-pane layouts which dynamically adapt their structures for tablets versus phones.6. Vendor-Specific StylesAdhering to the official interface guidelines of companies:Apple iOS Icons: Auto-styled with consistent shapes, standard resolutions, rounded corners, and polished shine effects.Microsoft Windows XP Fonts: Explicitly standardized to use Trebuchet for titles and Tahoma for body text.
